risks.note: Operating in a highly regulated sector requires consistent compliance with healthcare, labour, environmental, data and anti-corruption requirements; any breach can affect licenses, reputation and operating flexibility. Mitigated through a strengthened code of conduct, compliance training, whistle-blower mechanisms, internal controls, policy reviews, ethics oversight and periodic legal/compliance audits. Flagged as having negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Medical ethics, legal and regulatory compliance

risks.note: Hospitals handle sensitive patient and employee data; any unauthorised access, leak or cyber incident can result in legal exposure, regulatory scrutiny, service disruption and loss of trust. Mitigated via access controls, encryption, privileged-access management, backup and recovery protocols, vendor safeguards, awareness training, incident response and regular security audits. Negative financial implications.

Clinical staff face exposure to infections, sharps injuries, chemicals, radiation, patient-handling risks and fire/emergency hazards; a strong safety culture is essential to protect employees and ensure uninterrupted patient care. Mitigated through infection prevention and control protocols, PPE, safety training, emergency drills, incident reporting, root-cause review, vaccination support, ergonomic controls and periodic health surveillance. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Occupational health and safety of clinical staff

risks.note: Healthcare facilities generate biomedical, hazardous and domestic waste and are significant users of water; weak segregation, treatment or reuse practices can lead to non-compliance, reputational damage, infection risk and higher operating cost. Mitigated through strict segregation and labeling, authorised disposal via approved vendors, wastewater treatment and reuse, rainwater harvesting where feasible, 3R practices and periodic audits against pollution control requirements. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Water and waste management (hazardous and non-hazardous)

risks.note: Uninterrupted availability of medicines, consumables, diagnostics and equipment is critical in healthcare; poor supplier governance or concentration risk can affect service delivery and cost stability. Mitigation includes supplier due diligence, quality and ethical sourcing checks, critical inventory planning and an alternate sourcing strategy. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Responsible procurement and supply chain resilience

risks.note: The healthcare business is exposed to operational, clinical, regulatory, technology, supply and external shocks; a structured risk management framework is needed to reduce disruption and protect continuity of care. Mitigated by enterprise risk registers, mitigation-plan reviews with stakeholders, monitoring of critical dependencies, stress-testing of business continuity and disaster recovery plans, and periodic management reviews. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Enterprise risk management and business continuity

risks.note: Healthcare quality depends on the availability of skilled doctors, nurses, technicians and support staff. The BRSR discloses a permanent-employee turnover rate of 37% in FY2026 (34% male, 40% female), up from 35% in FY2025 and 33% in FY2024, with the Company noting FY2025-26 attrition data includes nursing exits with tenure of less than 3 months - a structural workforce-churn exposure for a consultant-led clinical model.
risks.risk: Talent attraction, retention and high employee attrition

risks.note: 100% of turnover comes from a single activity - human health activities / medical services (healthcare services) - and operations are confined to six states in India with no international locations and no export revenue, leaving the Company undiversified by both business line and geography.

sk.overview: The Indian healthcare delivery industry comprises government and private providers offering both in-patient (IPD) and out-patient (OPD) services across primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary care. The market is skewed towards private players due to limited government spending and overburdened state infrastructure, and remains highly fragmented, with large private hospitals accounting for only ~20% of the overall market in fiscal 2025.
